name: Lactic acid (gel or suppositories put in the vagina)
short: In the vagina: mild irritation and extra discharge reported; adverse events no different from placebo in one trial (125 women). No safety data in pregnancy were found (one 10-woman study).
text: This entry covers lactic acid gels and suppositories put in the vagina; no data on lactic acid taken by mouth are included. In a randomised trial of 125 women with bacterial vaginosis, adverse events did not differ between lactic acid suppositories, metronidazole by mouth and placebo (the abstract gives no figures). In a randomised trial of 518 women, side effects were reported less often with lactic acid gel than with metronidazole by mouth (nausea 8% versus 32%, taste changes 1% versus 18%, diarrhoea 6% versus 20%). In a 110-woman trial, women given vaginal lactic acid with metronidazole had only mild and tolerable vaginal irritation, as the authors describe it; in a 90-woman trial, one of 60 women given lactic acid gel reported increased curd-like discharge. In a 42-woman prevention trial the lactate gel was described as free of side effects. Outside bacterial vaginosis, an observational study of 72 women using lactic acid gel to prevent urinary infections recorded six mild adverse events, all resolved, and a study of 55 women without symptoms using a gel of lactic acid and glycogen reported a low incidence of mild adverse effects. Pregnancy: a study of 10 pregnant women with bacterial vaginosis treated with a vaginal lactate gel for 6 weeks reports no safety data, and no other pregnancy data were found in the cited sources. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
